event_model_payload.headline: Discord Begins Rolling Out Age Verification–And A Sponsorship With FanDuel
event_model_payload.summary:
Discord has officially begun rolling out age-verification measures as of today. The company first announced age verification--and, subsequently, limits placed on accounts of those under 18--back in February of this year, but delayed a full implementation until just recently.

According to the official announcement blog post, this delay was done in order to include more age-assurance options, including several that do not rely on controversial biometric or digital ID systems, which have raised privacy concerns--especially after a well-publicized hack exposed tens of thousands of Discord users' personal IDs. Instead, they are using an algorithmic combination of factors to determine user age, including how long your account has existed, the servers you're in, the games you play, and other factors, detailed in a technical blog published alongside the announcement. (However, this model is not available in all territories, such as the UK and Austrialia--both of which have enacted strict social media bans and age verification laws.)

While Discord assures users that "More than 90% of you won’t be asked to confirm your age," the company also acknowledge that their model isn't flawless, and some accounts will need to verify their age to use a non-age-restricted Discord account. If users want to avoid uploading ID or video, they can use services like Apple Pay, Google Play, Google Wallet, or AgeKey, or enter a credit card number.

With any attempt at age verification comes controversy, however, and users of Discord were quick to notice that age verification was rolling out at the exact same time as sponsored ads for sports betting website FanDuel were appearing for American users. Obviously, it's illegal to use FanDuel if you're under 21 (or 18 in some jurisdictions), so it didn't take much for social media users to assume a connection between the two events.

We have reached out to Discord for comment on the sponsorship, as well as other potential age-restricted product or service sponsorships in the future. A Discord spokesperson responded, "We’re taking a deliberate, user-first approach to evolving our ads business to add genuine value that connects naturally with our users' sports, gaming and entertainment interests.”

According to Discord, this sponsorship was a limited test in the United States and that "Discord’s policies still prohibit ads for traditional real-money gaming, including casinos and sportsbooks." It was also noted that "Daily Fantasy Sports ads, and FanDuel brand ads on Discord are intended for adults, and we are using a range of age signals to help ensure they are age appropriate. We use age group signals to exclude teens from seeing inappropriate ads and to make sure they have the right settings."

In the meantime, if you don't want to see sports betting ads on your Discord, go to Settings, then Data and Privacy, and scroll down to Sponsored Content. Then go to Manage Sponsored Content and choose to disable "Real Money Gaming." This will hopefully continue to work in the future for other advertising categories you may want to disable, as well.

event_model_payload.headline: Halo Stopped Being Relevant A Long Time Ago
event_model_payload.summary:
Halo: the flagship game of the Xbox brand. The #1 reason to buy an Xbox. The game that inspired countless clones and purported "Halo killers." All of this was true once upon a time. But the reality is that Halo's place in gaming today is not what its legacy would suggest.

Consider this--Halo has been irrelevant for longer than it was ever relevant. This realization dawned on me amid the Xbox "reset" news, and while it felt surprising to think about in those terms initially, it's true. Halo's peak lasted for about a decade: Combat Evolved released in 2001, and Reach closed out the Bungie era in 2010. It was around then that things started to go downhill.

The exact point at which things started to turn south differs from person to person: Was the brand diluted and beginning to become overexposed with the release of the exceedingly fine Halo Wars in 2009? Was it the mediocrity of 2013's Spartan Assault bearing the Halo name? The shoehorned-in Kinect support of Combat Evolved Anniversary in 2011?

For me at least, the cleanest answer is the departure of Bungie from the franchise, and more specifically, the moment that Halo 4 leaned into Call of Duty-style loadouts. (Reach introduced them, but 4's customization options made them more of a focal point.) It's at that point Halo felt cooked, as it began to imitate other games and follow trends rather than continuing to define its own identity (see: a major component of Halo 5 basically just being a multiplayer online battle arena game, and the numerous indications of a Halo battle royale mode being in the works over the years). 

It's hard to fathom now, but there was a time when Halo wasn't playing catch-up with its contemporaries and instead revolutionized first-person shooters, right down to the notion of only being able to carry two weapons at a time. Its sandboxes and multiplayer felt revelatory back in the early 2000s.

When's the last time you felt that way about anything in Halo? Infinite was the clearest vision of what a Halo game could be, with a fun campaign that tried to rethink the standard linear FPS format in an open-world setting--and even then, that structure was more reminiscent of other games, not something novel. Infinite's reworking of the battle-pass model to ditch the FOMO aspect was also nice--if somewhat of an indictment of the quality of the uninspired rewards, which wouldn't be worth a purchase if restricted to a limited-time window--but the mere presence of a battle pass in Halo in the first place felt, again, like trend chasing. 

In retrospect, it's no surprise that Infinite, and every other post-Bungie Halo game, failed to resonate as much as the earlier entries in the series. In that time, Modern Warfare catapulted Call of Duty clearly ahead of Halo and the franchise never looked back; battle royale games and extraction shooters came along and carved out significant markets of their own; Counter-Strike continued to do its thing; various games in the mold of Battlefield tried to nail that formula to varying degrees of success; classic shooters like Doom and Wolfenstein reinvented themselves to become better than ever; and Bungie again reimagined the first-person shooter with Destiny 1 and 2. 

What has Halo done in that span? What even defines a Halo game at this point? Would you recognize it without the name or Master Chief attached?

No doubt much or all of this can be traced back to poor management. Despite a 15-year span composed of far more disappointments than highlights for Halo, as someone who has adored the series, I am sorry to see Halo Studios gutted and the franchise handed off to Activision. Given Xbox's shifting focus, it's easy to worry that the next Halo game will feel more like Call of Duty than ever before, and the 343/Halo Studios era has amply demonstrated that Halo can only succeed by being its own thing.

It might be unfair to stack up the number of years in which Halo was relevant against those in which it was not. The impact of Halo extends well beyond the 2000s. But the days in which Halo was Xbox's flagship franchise--let alone something that felt special or worth looking forward to--are a thing of an increasingly distant past.

event_model_payload.headline: Rainbow Six Siege Dev On Competing With GTA 6 And Why There Are No Plans For Siege 2
event_model_payload.summary:
Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 releases this November, and it's expected to take up a lot of time and attention, leading some to worry how other games may fare in its wake. Ubisoft's Joshua Mills, the creative director for Rainbow Six Siege, said it's unquestionable that "you're going to take a hit when that drops."

"All of us are going to play it," Mills told The Game Business.

So what can Ubisoft do for Siege when GTA 6 comes out? He said, "It's about being smart and with your expectations so you can keep the team and HQ aligned." He said if the developers working on Siege see the game's player numbers drop, "they can get anxious." However, he observed that the effect on player numbers from a big competitor release is "generally temporary."

Whatever the case, Mills said the "golden rule" that Ubisoft operates by is by serving "the players who stay like kings and queens."

"We don’t go on vacation just because a competitor is swelling the market. We double down and reward those spending their valuable time with us," he said.

Siege's fourth season (of year 11) will release around the time that GTA 6 comes out in November 2026. Mills teased that there are "some unannounced surprises" that Ubisoft is not disclosing yet, but he said they will "make a splash."

Why there is no Siege 2, at least not yet

Also in the interview, Mills discussed why Ubisoft made Siege X--a new and improved version of the game--instead of Siege 2.

He said "fundamentally rebuilding our entire system is a mountain of work." What Ubisoft came up with in Siege X represents nothing "even close to the level of scale" that the team would aim for with a possible full-on Siege sequel that would "rebuild the entire game."

"The need for doing it is not necessarily there with the cost of shutting the lights off. Because you can’t possibly run both at the same time," Mills said. "You would need the expertise of the team that’s running the game to rebuild it. It’d be really difficult to do.”

The Siege franchise is set to expand further in 2027 with the release of Rainbow Six Siege Tactics, a turn-based tactical game set in the Rainbow Six universe.

event_model_payload.headline: 30 Years Later, Collecting Pokemon Cards Hits A Little Different
event_model_payload.summary:
Let me sound like an old for a second.

I remember in the late '90s and early '00s, collecting Pokemon cards was a casual hobby. You'd go to your local brick-and-mortar store with the money you made from mowing the lawn or whatever, drop maybe $10 on a couple of packs, rip them open, then go to your middle school to trade cards with your friends. No one knew how to actually play the game; the cards just looked cool, and everyone wanted something. Me? I wanted a holographic Charizard, and I would've traded literally anything to get my hands on such a rarity.

It was so low-key back in the day. Saying that grosses me out, as I sound like a Boomer or Gen Xer, but it's true: Collecting Pokemon cards wasn't that serious, and we didn't put much stock in the cards, stuffing them in bags or pockets and watching them turn up in washing machines.

Now? Things are totally different. You can't just collect Pokemon cards as a hobbyist anymore. You've got to fight with scalpers looking to make a quick buck off nostalgia, as well as the kids who are either getting into the TCG for the first time or hoping to get something tradeable for their friends. (I don't decry the kids. They're not at fault.)

There have been plenty of incidents involving card collecting and violence lately. Robbers stole over $100,000 in rare cards from a California store in December 2025. A different set of robbers made off with nearly $120,000 in rare cards at gunpoint in New York in January 2026. Police broke up a chaotic Costco scene over Prismatic Evolutions in April 2026. And more recently, a Connecticut man was arrested for assaulting someone in a Target after being confronted for exceeding the store's limit for Pokemon card packs, while a 72-year-old Ohio man pleaded guilty to using a GPS tracker to stalk a woman stocking Pokemon cards.

I get it--and I don't. The cards look cool, with fabulous designs on weighty cardstock. Sometimes there are alternate versions of the same card that have a fuller design, like a tiny piece of artwork, instead of just an illustration of the Pokemon that takes up a tiny rectangle. Collecting them for this reason, them being tiny pieces of artwork, makes sense.

I also understand the value of the cards, with many of them going for hundreds--if not thousands--of dollars on resale sites like eBay. It's a great way to make some money in this economy, especially if you have vintage cards that aren't being pressed and printed anymore.

But turning toward violence because you "gotta collect 'em all" or whatever is silly at best and petulant at worst. This is a children's hobby. That's what all of my friends did in middle school (even though we were all partial to Yu-Gi-Oh). I get that Pokemon is celebrating 30 years this year, but there's absolutely no reason to resort to violence--like shooting someone--over some illustrated cardstock. Besides, do these people even know how to play the Pokemon TCG? I didn't (still don't), and neither did my friends growing up.

That's perhaps my main takeaway from all of these chaotic and violent incidents. No one even knows how to play the game, so why are we taking collecting so seriously? The answer is obvious--money--but what we're robbing is kids' enjoyment of a hobby we barely understood ourselves. When you can only take one, you should only take one. Leave the rest for your son or daughter. They might be trying to trade their friends for that one card to complete their collection, and that's the real joy.

event_model_payload.headline: High On Life Is Helping Make The Case For Bigger Games On Quest
event_model_payload.summary:
High on Life has been a big hit since it first launched in 2022, thanks to its bizarre sense of humor, motor-mouthed guns, and polished gameplay. But can it succeed as a virtual reality port? That's the question Flat2VR is aiming to answer, as the team behind several VR games is now working with Squanch Games to bring High on Life to Meta Quest 3 and 3S headsets. 

While it's still early days for the project, I took the time to chat to High on Life VR game director Emily O'Neal and Eric Masher, co-founder and chief operating officer for Impact Reality and Flat2VR Studios, about this project and the challenges involved in adapting it for a new platform.

And yes, Knifey did make his way into the conversation.

So why VR? High on Life has been available on PC and console for several years now, but it is considered a smaller, niche platform--or so you'd think, as Masher explained that the VR user base has grown considerably over the years. "VR is a smaller market; it doesn't mean that it's a small market," Masher said. "You know, we're looking at numbers now of Quest headsets being in the 30-million to 40-million range. Those are not numbers to take lightly. A game like Gorilla Tag--which is a free-to-play game--has done over $100 million in revenue. We do see that audience that has been playing Gorilla Tag starting to grow up. They started when they were younger kids, and now they're getting older and have disposable income. What are they going to want to play next?"

"We want to bring them those high-quality games like High on Life, that [have] more teeth, more depth, and more playability as an actual game. We're not here just for a short snapshot in time; we're here to help grow this industry to where it will be in three to five years from now. Our job and our mission at Flat2VR is to bring the immersive, amazing games that you love playing right now on your console and PC, but bring it to another platform that makes a whole bunch of sense and that feels completely different but still the same.”

Bringing High on Life to VR isn't an easy task either, as you can't just press a "Convert to VR" button for a project of this scale. As O'Neal explained, the original game is massive, and the team is looking to make it run as smoothly as possible on a VR headset.

"There are a ton of animations and wildly different worlds, so even getting that much data to fit on a standalone platform is a big challenge," O'Neal explained. "You have to load it all in a decent amount of time and run it in real time, ideally at 72 frames per second. All of that optimization represents a cluster of problems our tech-art teams are chipping away at from many angles. A huge part of our technical challenge has been upgrading the game to a more modern version of Unreal Engine. Modernizing our toolsets allows us to perform the optimizations needed to get these massive, gorgeous, colorful worlds running on Meta Quest. That covers the core issue: the sheer scale of the game and optimizing it to fit on the headset while maintaining frame rate."

O'Neal added that the team wants players to poke and prod the Gatlian firearms they collect in the game, and they represent an incredible design challenge thanks to their expressive facial details and complex skeletons used to make them emote. "The Gatlians are without a doubt my favorite part of the game. When defining the mission statement for the VR adaptation, they are 100% the centerpiece. The core question we continually return to with every feature is: Do you feel like you're holding a living creature in your hand, and when they speak to you, do you feel like you're truly interacting with them? Because the Gatlians are the main characters, they are our highest priority."

"A huge part of that focus goes into the gunplay since they serve as your weapons. With any VR first-person shooter, how you handle reloading is vital--whether that's a realistic manual reload, a simple button press, bringing the weapon to your hip, or providing options for all of the above. While our design team has built reload mechanics many times before, designing them for the Gatlians has been uniquely fun because of their distinct body shapes and personalities. We look at the unique physical traits of each alien, considering not just function, but how players can fidget and interact with them while listening to in-game dialogue. Ultimately, the Gatlians are the defining feature of the VR port because they are in your hands the entire time."

Out of all the Gatlians, Knifey is arguably the breakout star of the High on Life arsenal. A sentient blade with an unmatched bloodthirst, O'Neal teased that the murder-happy melee tool is a big focus of the team. "Yes, Knifey is 100% getting the most treatment out of the whole cast," O'Neal said. "There's a huge gap between pressing a button to trigger a knife slash versus making that motion yourself, so some of the biggest new systems we're building are specifically for Knifey.

"His whole personality revolves around pure bloodlust—he's constantly begging you to use him and stab things—so we're leaning hard into that. We're building new VR-specific systems to capture that visceral feeling of stabbing Knifey into flesh. It's not a gory game and won't feel like one; we're maintaining the same comedy and humor with all of Knifey's interactions, but leaning into mechanics you can only achieve with a knife in VR. Most importantly, we want a Knifey-first strategy to be a genuinely viable way to play the entire game, so we're spending a lot of time with him."

One of the other challenges with virtual reality, especially games with a variety of fast-paced movement systems like High on Life, is the looming spectre of motion sickness. Some people don't suffer from it; others are ready to hurl chunks after a few minutes of Pistol Whip. But as Masher explained, the High on Life VR team is going all out on providing options that help players fine-tune the game to their tastes.

"We take comfort super seriously. The real power fantasy lies in the traversal abilities you get with the bounty suit, so we don't want to sacrifice or remove any of that from the game, but we do want it to be approachable to anyone who wants to play," Masher explained. "The first piece of that is performance: It has to be stable, responsive, and hit its target frame rate. That's the foundational element to ensure people don't get motion sick. Beyond that, we're going all out on options. As a team of people who love and play VR in our free time, we offer the full suite of accessibility settings you'd expect in a VR title--from snap turn and smooth turn to custom smooth turning speeds--so players can tune the experience to whatever feels comfortable for their body. The goal is to let players dial in their preferences to minimize the discomfort that can come from smooth movement and turning."

Masher also added that motion sickness was something we could hear much less about in the future, as, thanks to a generation of young users growing up with VR headsets, the immersive nature of games on that hardware was something they'd become accustomed to. "What's nice about motion sickness is that we're starting to see it become less prominent, especially with younger players. Years ago, VR was a niche hobby where you were probably 20 or 30 years old before putting on your first headset. That's no longer the case--kids are growing up in VR headsets now, with games like Gorilla Tag introducing kids as young as 10 or 11 to the platform.

"They know nothing but gaming inside a VR headset, so by the time they grow up, it's completely normal for them. It's almost like we're breeding motion sickness out of the audience. You're either susceptible or you're not, but if VR is all you've ever known, motion sickness just isn't an issue. So I'm hopeful it becomes a thing of the past. Plus, as Emily noted, hardware getting better and making higher frame rates easier to hit makes a massive difference."

High on Life VR doesn’t have a release date yet, but you can preorder it now through the Meta Horizon Store.

event_model_payload.headline: Arc Raiders’ Battle Pass Won’t Be Totally Free Anymore, But It’ll Pay For Itself
event_model_payload.summary:
When Arc Raiders' next major update, Frozen Trail, goes live on October 8, it'll introduce lots of changes and additions, and while the update itself will be free, the new battle pass system that comes with it won't be--at least not entirely.

To date, Arc Raiders has featured three battle pass-like Raider Decks in the game. Players could complete dailies to unlock Creds that then got them rewards like new cosmetics and in-game items. With Frozen Trail, Embark Studios' new Reward Pass is replacing this system with one quite like it, only it'll also have a paid premium track for unlocking additional rewards.

Anyone who owns the game gets the Free Pass, naturally, while the paid track will cost 1,150 Raider Tokens, or about $10 USD. Thankfully, Embark is taking the opportunity to sort the rewards responsibly, with the Premium Pass offering only cosmetic items. Players will get gameplay-altering items, like new weapons and gear, exclusively through the Free Pass. This approach avoids any type of pay-to-win debacle.

Maybe the best feature of the newly priced Reward Pass is that if you buy access to the Premium Pass, you'll earn back more than you spent on it, pocketing 1,350 Raider Tokens for completing the pass, 200 of which are found in the Free Pass. Of course, your time isn't free either, but since Arc Raiders was my Game of the Year last year, I'm happy to see that sort of player-friendly exchange rate debut in Arc Raiders, especially after it recently left my other live-service favorite, Fortnite.

Along with the new Reward Pass, Frozen Trail seems poised to reset Arc Raiders in a major way, with the frosty Pendola Pass map adding a lot to both gameplay and lore, taking raiders where they've never dwelled before and stumbling upon several new Arc threats: the Bully, Skulker, and Hydra. 

The Frigate is a new airborne carrier and raid-like event that's designed to take several players most of a round to overcome through combat and puzzles. Aboard the Frigate, the Hydra awaits, capable of downing multiple players at a time and even respawning once it's defeated. 

Weapon amplification will give players new ways to customize their weapons, disrupting the meta and challenging players to try new loadouts, while stencils act like weapon skins, offering new cosmetic changes to guns. 

As for gameplay items, Frozen Trail adds the banjo and harmonica instruments, a camera, and a grappling hook, which is sure to be a new community favorite.

Of course, another big Arc Raiders update means more quests, and now they'll offer optional objectives for added rewards. Skill trees are also being overhauled to both add new skills and alter existing ones.

The update also adds Outposts, new customizable areas for raiders to call their own. As for an explorable Speranza, Embark's Aleksander Grondal said that it's still something the team is looking into, though no such addition will be available with the Frozen Trail launch.

"So that's been a question we have been asked a few times, and it's something that we have looked at and discussed a number of times," Grondal said during a roundtable interview. "And at the moment, there is none of that, but we could see a future where you could invite your friends into your Outposts, for instance, as something that we want to try. We see the need for a place to socialize and kind of hang out between the raids, but we really haven't settled on exactly how we want to execute against that need yet; it's something that is [at the] top of our list when we think about where to take Arc Raiders next."

Grondal confirmed the team is still working on the idea of major updates roughly every six months, though the next big update following Frozen Trail doesn't have a set date yet. In May, Grondal told me that some on the team were "a little bit uncomfortable" about the pivot to a new roadmap. I asked him how the team is feeling now that Frozen Trail is nearly here. He explained that it brings up a mix of emotions.

"If you take a look at where we were when we did the monthly updates and where we are today, we feel a lot better about what we're putting out [and the] quality we're putting into the updates. So I think the team feels good about that. Of course, it's scary every time we do a big update. To me, the best way to describe it is that it almost feels like we're shipping the game again, because I get flashbacks to last year when we were in this very same position trying to make the game complete.

"So it becomes almost scarier in a way because the updates are larger and, of course, more complicated to execute. I think, overall, the team is pretty happy and excited to share what we've been working on basically since May of this year, and yeah, I'm also excited."

Frozen Trail comes to Arc Raiders on October 8 as a free update on all platforms. When it goes live, the new Frozen Trail Collector Set shop bundle will include a new outfit, weapon stencil, hairstyle, and 2,400 Raider Tokens, plus instant access to the Premium Pass.

event_model_payload.headline: Grab Resident Evil 4 Remake For Less Than $10 Right Now, Making It Cheaper Than Ever
event_model_payload.summary:
Leon Kennedy might be one of the coolest horror game protagonists. With that iconic curtain hairstyle with layered length, blocking chainsaws with a knife, and doing completely unnecessary backflips out of danger, he’s an action hero in the wrong genre, and that’s exactly why he remains a fan-favorite main character. While the second game introduced us to Mr. Kennedy, Resident Evil 4 made him who he is today, and now you can play one of the best Resident Evil games for less than $10, with its beautiful remake at its lowest price ever.

What I love about the Resi games is that, despite having an overarching narrative, you can play any entry at any point in your life, and almost all of them are solid starting points. My first Resident Evil game was 5, and I never played 4 until I was around 19. Yeah, I left it quite some time ago—about 10 years—and I was enamored with its stronger survival horror elements. Now, well, Resident Evil 4’s remake has taken the throne as my favorite entry because it’s a faithful recreation that delivers more action, more scares, and more Leon Kennedy.

In Resi 4, Leon Kennedy is a more worn-down face following the events of Raccoon City. As an agent for the United States government, he’s sent to a rural village in Spain to save the president’s kidnapped daughter, Ashley, only to find a cult-like setup involving people infected and controlled by a parasite called Las Plagas. Frustratingly, Leon ends up getting injected with the parasite himself, which makes things a little more difficult.

In familiar Resident Evil fashion, which was strengthened by the 2005 original, Resident Evil 4 sees you take on hordes of infected people in the typical third-person shooter manner. Resources are scarce, death is likely, and being scared is almost definite. Between surviving enemies in tense situations, puzzles will keep your brain ticking as you try to find Ashley and, hopefully, find a cure for the little parasite problem you have.

The original Resident Evil 4, much like Requiem did over two decades later, nailed the balance between horror and action. While Resi 5 and 6 moved towards the latter, before 7 and Village went full whammy into horror again, Resident Evil 4, and its eventual remake, delivered the best of both worlds, Hannah Montana-style.

If you’re looking to give the remake a try, now’s a great opportunity, as you can grab the new take on Resident Evil 4 for just $8.79 / £7.69 at Fanatical. That’s an absolute bargain, and for one of the best horror games of recent years (and technically, ever), this is a deal that’s hard to ignore. Honestly, I paid full price for it and had a great time.

event_model_payload.headline: Marvel’s Wolverine Claws Are Real Now, And Your Groceries Don’t Stand A Chance
event_model_payload.summary:
Contrary to comic book science, you don't need to enroll in a shadowy Canadian black-ops program and undergo excruciating pain to get a set of Wolverine's signature claws. Instead, it's much easier--and less traumatic--to simply hire some blacksmiths to craft you a set, which is exactly what PlayStation did to celebrate the launch of Marvel's Wolverine. Choosing Fiedlero Knives for the job, PlayStation tasked the blacksmith with creating a custom set of Wolverine-inspired claws, and unsurprisingly, the end result looks downright lethal.

They may not be made of indestructible adamantium, but these blades made short work of some fresh produce when tested. And best of all, you don't need a mutant healing factor to wield these--although it would be advisable, just in case you equip them and accidentally trip. Similar to the practical props used by Hugh Jackman, these claws are attached to a handle that makes the blades look like they're really coming out of your hands. Plenty of knock-offs are available online, including plastic versions that are slightly safer than the metal ones.

Marvel's Wolverine launched earlier this month, but the reception has been lukewarm at best. The game has been criticized for its restrictive level design, excessive hand-holding, and repetitive combat, but developer Insomniac Games is aiming to address these complaints. A new patch for the game recently went live, toning down the intrusive scent trails and audio cues that lead to collectibles within the various levels.

"At best, it’s a fun but forgettable experience that’ll entertain you for a few hours. At worst, it shows that just because you can make really good superhero games with one character, that doesn’t mean you can make really good superhero games with any character," Tamoor Hussain wrote in GameSpot's Marvel's Wolverine review.

While that set of custom Wolverine claws aren't for sale, you can get your hands on a sixth-scale replica of the unstoppable mutant from Hot Toys. It comes with several sets of smaller claws to equip him with, as well as an impressive amount of accurate body hair on his beefy silicone arms.

event_model_payload.headline: Star Wars Zero Company Reportedly Hits 1 Million Sales, But Will It Be Enough?
event_model_payload.summary:
Star Wars Zero Company released in late August, and the game has evidently found an audience, as market-data firm Alinea Analytics estimates that the game has sold 1 million units.

Writing on Twitter, analyst Rhys Elliott shared the estimate, which heavily favors PC. Roughly 70% of sales were on PC--unsurprising given the turn-based-tactics genre--with PlayStation following at roughly 20% and Xbox at about 10%. Elliott called its performance thus far "respectable for the genre and during such a crowded period" that also saw the launch of games like Onimusha: Way of the Sword and The Blood of Dawnwalker.

Elliott also noted, however, that Zero Company's appeal is almost entirely to Western audiences, with less than 5% of the game's players being in Asia.

The news comes weeks after developer Bit Reactor furloughed a large portion of its staff, and it isn't yet clear when or if they will be able to resume their work at the studio. Having Zero Company perform well commercially would presumably make publisher EA more interested in a sequel, but it also comes at a very strange time for the company, which was just taken private as part of a deal with the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund.

Regardless, Star Wars Zero Company is definitely worth playing if you're a fan of XCOM-style games. In our 8/10 Star Wars Zero Company review, Steve Watts said, "Developer Bit Reactor set higher ambitions than simply slapping a Star Wars skin on a template," praising its tweaks to the XCOM formula.

event_model_payload.headline: Resident Evil Movie Director Reveals His Four Favorite Games
event_model_payload.summary:
Zach Cregger, the director of the newly released Resident Evil movie, has revealed his top four favorite video games, and he made some solid choices.

Before he listed off his top four to Regal, Cregger said they came "off the top of my head," so if he had more time, he might have chosen other games. Or he may not have. In any event, here are the games that Cregger singled out as his four faves:

  • The Binding Of Isaac
  • Dark Souls 3
  • Resident Evil 4
  • The Last of Us 2

People are saying that Cregger earned his "gamer cred" for these specific choices (via GamesRadar). His Dark Souls 3 pick was not surprising given Cregger was known to stream the game on Twitch over the years. It's also not surprising that he called out Resident Evil 4, as he borrowed from that game for his movie. In the same interview, Resident Evil actor Austin Abrams, who plays Bryan, said Cregger asked him to play Resident Evil 2, 4, and 7 to prepare for the movie.

Cregger received a lot of backlash from core fans of the Resident Evil series over the direcion he took the movie and how it didn't feature any stories or characters from the games. He said he was naive to think fans would embrace his ideas. Things seemed to work out for Cregger in the end, as Resident Evil scored fantastic reviews and had a gigantic opening weekend at the box office.

"Bethesda will expand its remit to include Obsidian, which will continue its current projects, including Grounded, as well as the new Fallout project made in collaboration with Bethesda Game Studios," Booty wrote on Xbox Wire.

Obsidian Entertainment--which developed copious RPGs from Neverwinter Nights 2 to Pillars of Eternity to Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords to The Outer Worlds--lost 25% of its staff in July after Xbox's first major reset. This resulted in the Avowed sequel being killed and the acclaimed RPG studio shifting its focus to the Fallout franchise, with a new game in development. It's unclear if this project is Fallout 5 or some spin-off of the long-running series, but alongside whatever Obsidian Entertainment is working on, there are at least three Fallout pies in the oven now.

event_model_payload.headline: Nighthawks review – a series of vignettes that sometimes excel but more often falter
event_model_payload.summary:
Nighthawks, the 1942 painting by Edward Hopper, is generally described as portraying loneliness. The four people at the diner counter are dwarfed by the empty, cold openness of the street. But the inside of the diner looks warm. One man sits apart, but the other two patrons might be a couple, their hands close. The worker seems to be watching them, perhaps thinking of somebody he’ll return to after his shift. Nighthawks, the 2026 vampire RPG, takes this same sensation, connection in the middle of isolation, and plays it much less subtly. When it works, it manages to tell sub-stories that will stick with me like the glow of a friendly building late at night.

But it doesn’t always work.

event_model_payload.headline: Silent Hill: Townfall review - an often inspired, if slightly lumbering trek into the fog
event_model_payload.summary:
Once a fictional town in Maine, Silent Hill has broken containment and become a transferable oral history mechanism, offered to videogame developers worldwide as a way of investigating, even celebrating local culture. I'm still in two minds about whether this licensing outreach project, begun with Silent Hill f, is more inspired than it is vampiric. I picture Konami's invitation being pushed under the door of potential collaborators like Mary's letter to James in Silent Hill 2: "in our restless dreams, we see that town... let's touch base there sometime, expand our concepts further."

There's opportunity and peril for any studio who answers the letter: opportunity, because Silent Hill is an uncommonly rich way of thinking about the past, with its parallel realities, monster metaphors, and woozy grounding in both mysticism and psychoanalysis. And peril, because licenses have a way of engulfing licensees, forcing them into a straitjacket of tropes: fog, sirens, antagonists with geometric heads. Thankfully, Silent Hill: Townfall's creators Screen Burn (previously No Code) haven't gotten lost in the murk, though I don't think Townfall is their finest creation, not least because it's overreliant on stealth. Like the makers of Silent Hill f, they've taken what they need from Silent Hill to tell a story of their own.

event_model_payload.headline: Single player games might require age verification if they use Steam under EU Kids Act's current draft, according to MEP's senior policy adviser
event_model_payload.summary:
The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The draft legislation is called the EU Kids Act and calls for the setting up of a tiered system governing the types of accounts children under 15 can create to access such services, enforced by mandatory age verification for all users.

The documents laying out the proposal have been officially released, and based on the current wording the Commission have used to define what they class as an online game, it seems single player games that rely on online platforms like Steam for updates, distribution, or even a one-time authentication could be caught in the crossfire. That is, unless the definition is tightened up before the law is set in stone, if it indeed it makes it that far.

event_model_payload.headline: "Publishers are afraid of certain parts of the world": Saber Interactive's message to North American studios is to get their head out of their own geography
event_model_payload.summary:
Layoffs have been a constant drumbeat in gaming industry news since 2022. Even if the cadence of layoffs seems to have slowed in 2026, the severity of those cuts has not lessened. In July, Microsoft made 1600 staff redundant as part of its great reset, and promised investors they would let 1600 more staff go in the next 12 months.

Cuts like those and the ongoing economic pressures plaguing the industry – rising debt rates, a cost of living crisis, and a memory shortage that is making every aspect of making and playing video games pricier – should have the head of any large studio examining their plans for the future. Especially when games are taking longer to make, costing more to make, and up against a much greater volume of competition than even two years ago.

With all that in mind, when I wasn't talking to Saber Interactive's chief creative officer Tim Willits about generative AI, I wanted to know what he would do if he ran one of those 200-people big-budget game studios. Because say what you like about Saber (and there's a lot of things people like to say about Saber), but the developer is doing well at a time when a lot of other studios and publishers are struggling.
